{{Short description|Compact subset of the complex plane}}
{{Other uses|Swiss cheese (disambiguation)}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''Swiss cheese''' is a [[compact space|compact]] [[subset]] of the [[complex plane]] obtained by removing from a [[disc (mathematics)|closed disc]] some countably infinite [[union (set theory)|union]] of [[disc (mathematics)|open discs]], usually with some restriction on the centres and radii of the removed discs. Traditionally the deleted discs should have pairwise [[disjoint sets|disjoint]] [[closure (topology)|closures]] which are subsets of the [[interior (topology)|interior]] of the starting disc, the sum of the radii of the deleted discs should be finite, and the Swiss cheese should have [[empty set|empty]] interior. This is the type of Swiss cheese originally introduced by the Swiss mathematician [[Alice Roth]].

More generally, a Swiss cheese may be all or part of [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> &ndash; or of an even more complicated [[manifold]] &ndash; with "holes" in it.
